morphology.capsule: No capsule; a resistant cyst wall forms in the cyst stage
morphology.motility: Motile via pseudopods in the trophozoite stage; the cyst stage is non-motile

habitat.hostAssociation: Obligate parasite of humans and some primates; cysts are the infective, environmentally resistant stage
habitat.environmentalOccurrence: Cysts can survive in contaminated water and food, particularly in areas with poor sanitation
habitat.reservoir: Human intestinal tract — asymptomatic cyst passers are the main reservoir

microscopy.stain: Iodine wet mount; trichrome stain of stool
microscopy.appearance: Trophozoite: amoeboid, with ingested red blood cells (erythrophagocytosis) diagnostic of active dysentery. Cyst: round, with 1-4 nuclei
microscopy.arrangement: Single organisms seen on stool smear

culture.media: Not routinely cultured in clinical labs; specialized media used only in research settings
culture.colonyMorphology: Not applicable — not colony-forming on standard media

identificationClues: Trophozoites with ingested red blood cells (erythrophagocytosis) on stool microscopy — the hallmark of invasive disease
Quadrinucleate cysts on stool ova-and-parasite exam
Flask-shaped ulcers on colonoscopy or histology
Anchovy-paste appearance of liver abscess aspirate
Must be distinguished from the morphologically identical, non-pathogenic Entamoeba dispar

diseases: Rare extraintestinal spread to lung or brain
virulenceFactors: Galactose/N-acetylgalactosamine (Gal/GalNAc) lectin — mediates adhesion to colonic mucosa
Amoebapores — pore-forming proteins that cause cytolysis
clinicalImportance.transmission: Fecal-oral route — ingestion of mature cysts in contaminated food or water
clinicalImportance.epidemiology: Common in areas with poor sanitation; a leading parasitic cause of death worldwide, after malaria and schistosomiasis
clinicalImportance.labSignificance: Stool antigen testing or PCR is needed to distinguish pathogenic E. histolytica from the morphologically identical, non-pathogenic E. dispar

examFacts.keyBiochemicalReaction: Not a biochemical-test organism — diagnosed by stool microscopy, antigen testing, or PCR
examFacts.importantTest: Stool O&P exam for RBC-containing trophozoites; stool antigen ELISA
examFacts.distinguishingFeature: Trophozoites containing ingested red blood cells distinguish invasive disease from simple colonization
